checkpoints.title: When Retrieval Is Useful
checkpoints.summary: Choose cleanly between prompt context stuffing, RAG, SQL/API lookup, and fine-tuning—never force vector RAG where a SQL query wins.
learningObjectives: Compare RAG vs long-context prompts vs structured DB queries vs fine-tuning.
Use RAG for large, evolving unstructured corpora (help centers, policies, manuals).
Avoid vector search for exact relational aggregations (`count open invoices` belongs in SQL!).
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose you have 15 short refund rules (~2 pages total): just pass them directly in the prompt—setting up an embedding pipeline and vector database would be pure overkill! Suppose instead a customer asks about their exact invoice total: run a deterministic **SQL or CRM API lookup**, never semantic vector guesses! **RAG (Retrieval-Augmented Generation)** shines specifically when you have hundreds or thousands of changing unstructured documents (help docs, SOPs, product manuals) and need only the top relevant passages cited per question.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Evaluate four data patterns before building vector pipelines: (1) Small static corpus (<10k tokens) -> direct context / prompt caching; (2) Exact structured numbers/records -> deterministic SQL/REST query; (3) Large, frequently changing, permission-scoped unstructured docs -> RAG; (4) Consistent domain style/format -> fine-tuning (NEVER use fine-tuning to store changing business policies or enforce tenant permissions!).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Overusing vector RAG for small docs wastes infra complexity, while misusing RAG for SQL aggregations produces wrong totals.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Adopt RAG for changing multi-document unstructured knowledge needing freshness, low context noise, tenant ACLs, and source citations.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Skip vector databases when docs easily fit cleanly in a cached system prompt, OR when deterministic SQL/API filters answer exact structured queries better.

checkpoints.title: Document Loading
checkpoints.summary: Extract clean structured text, headings, and source metadata from Markdown, HTML, and PDFs—filtering navigation noise at ingestion.
learningObjectives: Load clean text while stripping HTML navbars, cookie banners, and email boilerplate.
Preserve structural hierarchy (title, section headings, URL, `updated_at`, ACL tags).
Handle dirty PDFs/tables thoughtfully instead of feeding broken whitespace into embeddings.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Garbage in, garbage out hits RAG harder than almost anything else! If your web scraper loads every Help Center article *including* the cookie banner, top navigation links, sidebar menu, and copyright footer, half your vector database embeds identical website navigation instead of the actual refund rule. Clean document loaders strip boilerplate deterministically and save rich metadata (`doc_id`, `url`, `section_title`, `updated_at`, `audience`) alongside clean text.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Design ingestion pipelines cleanly: parse HTML via semantic main-content extraction (`<article>`/`<main>`), preserve Markdown headings (`#`, `##`) as structural metadata, normalize Unicode/whitespace, and validate extracted PDF tables/columns visually on representative messy docs before bulk indexing. Assign a stable deterministic `source_doc_id` and `content_hash` so incremental syncs detect unchanged vs edited vs deleted documents cleanly.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Most RAG hallucinations and bad search matches trace directly back to messy ingestion (broken PDF tables, scraped cookie banners, lost headings).
checkpoints.whenToUse: Build a repeatable, test-covered document normalization pipeline before running any embedding job.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't dump raw scraped HTML tags or uncleaned OCR noise straight into your chunker.

examples.title: Clean Normalized Document Ingestion Record
examples.description: Inspect normalized text + hash + stable doc metadata before chunking.
examples.code:
import hashlib
from pydantic import BaseModel

class CleanSourceDoc(BaseModel):
    doc_id: str
    title: str
    source_url: str
    audience: str  # e.g. 'customer_public' | 'internal_only'
    updated_at: str
    body_markdown: str

    @property
    def content_hash(self) -> str:
        return hashlib.sha256(self.body_markdown.encode("utf-8")).hexdigest()[:16]

options.text: So incremental syncs only re-chunk and re-embed documents whose content actually changed, saving money and keeping deletes clean.
options.explanation: Correct! Hash-based change detection keeps sync pipelines fast and clean.

options.text: Because vector stores require SHA-256 passwords per paragraph.
options.explanation: Hashing tracks content changes efficiently.

checkpoints.title: Chunking
checkpoints.summary: Split documents along natural sections with controlled overlap and contextual headers so chunks stay self-contained instead of severed mid-rule.
learningObjectives: Explain why chunk size balances precision (too large = noisy) vs completeness (too small = cut off mid-sentence).
Prefer structure-aware chunking (Markdown headings/paragraphs) with modest overlap over blind fixed character splits.
Prepend document/section title context to every chunk so pronouns like `'it'` don't lose meaning.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose an FAQ page says `## Enterprise Plan Cancellation` followed by `'Cancellations require 30 days notice.'` If a blind character splitter puts the heading in Chunk 1 and `'Cancellations require 30 days notice'` in Chunk 2, searching `'Enterprise cancellation notice'` misses Chunk 2 OR retrieves Chunk 2 without knowing which plan it applies to! **Structure-aware chunking** splits at headings/paragraphs and injects the heading context (`[Doc: Billing FAQ > Enterprise Cancellation]`) right into each chunk.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Evaluate chunking strategies against real user queries: Markdown/HTML structure-aware splitters break along headings first, then recursively split oversized sections (~300–600 tokens target with ~10–15% overlap as a starting baseline—tuned by retrieval evals!). Injecting hierarchical breadcrumbs (`title > heading`) into stored chunk text dramatically improves semantic and keyword matching on ambiguous subsections.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Smart chunking + heading injection often improves RAG accuracy more than swapping expensive embedding models.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Split cleanly at semantic/heading boundaries, attach document + section title headers inside chunks, and verify chunk readability manually.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never pick arbitrary chunk parameters blindly (e.g. `chunk_size=100`) without inspecting actual resulting chunks on 10 real queries.

examples.title: Context-Preserving Section Chunking
examples.description: Prepend doc title and section breadcrumb so every retrieved chunk makes sense standalone.

Includes contextual document/section prefix inside chunks.

commonMistakes: Chopping mid-sentence or mid-Markdown-table with naive character offsets.
Indexing subsections like `'Timeframe: 14 days'` without prepending which policy/product header it belongs to!
Never reading 20 actual chunks on disk after running the chunker.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why inject `[Document: Billing Policy | Section: Annual Plan Refunds]` at the top of every text chunk before embedding?

options.text: Standalone passages containing pronouns or conditions (`'Within 14 days...'`) otherwise lose what plan/product they apply to—hurting BOTH retrieval and LLM answers.
options.explanation: Correct! Contextual headers make every chunk self-contained.

options.text: To double vector dimensions.
options.explanation: Dimensions depend on the embedding model.

options.text: Because JSON forbids paragraphs without brackets.
options.explanation: Contextualization improves semantic clarity.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep every chunk self-contained with its document and section context.

quizQuestions.prompt: What problem occurs if `chunk_size` is tiny (e.g., 40 tokens) vs huge (4,000 tokens)?

options.text: Tiny chunks lose surrounding qualifications/exceptions; huge chunks dilute vector similarity with irrelevant topics and waste prompt tokens.
options.explanation: Correct! Tune chunk size via retrieval Recall@K against real queries.

options.text: Tiny chunks disable TLS.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

options.text: Huge chunks always run faster.
options.explanation: Huge chunks add context noise and generation latency.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Balance chunk granularity using retrieval evaluations.

checkpoints.title: Embeddings
checkpoints.summary: Understand how embedding models convert meaning into numeric vectors—and why you MUST never mix different embedding models between index and query.
learningObjectives: Explain dense vector embeddings conceptually (similar meanings sit near each other in vector space).
Remember the golden operational rule: ingestion and query MUST use the exact same embedding model + version!
Know what embeddings miss (exact error codes, SKUs, acronyms—solved by hybrid search).
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: An embedding model turns a text chunk like *'How do I cancel my monthly subscription?'* into a list of numbers (e.g., 1,536 floats) representing its semantic location on a meaning map—so even if a policy doc says *'Ending your recurring plan'*, their coordinates land close together! **Critical catch:** embedding Model A and embedding Model B draw completely incompatible maps. If you swap embedding models for queries without re-embedding your stored chunks, search results turn into random noise!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Embedding models encode variable-length text into fixed-dimension dense vectors (`R^d`) normalized commonly for cosine similarity / dot-product ranking. Operational invariants: store `embedding_model_id` cleanly alongside index metadata and plan full index rebuild/backfill pipelines whenever upgrading embedding models. Also understand dense vectors blur exact lexical anchors (`ERR_AUTH_4012`, `SKU-9918`), motivating BM25/keyword hybrid retrieval.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Silently upgrading an embedding model on queries while old chunks stay embedded with yesterday's model breaks RAG search completely.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Record `embedding_model_id` on every index collection and trigger clean re-indexing whenever changing models.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never query an existing vector collection with a different embedding model (even same dimension count!) without re-indexing.

examples.title: Embedding Model Version Guard
examples.description: Record active embedding model in collection metadata to prevent mismatched vector searches.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Explain in your own words why querying `'ERR_509_GATEWAY'` often fails with pure dense embeddings and why switching embedding models requires re-embedding stored chunks.
acceptanceCriteria: Explains embeddings as semantic coordinate vectors.
Enforces matching embedding model between ingestion and query.
Recognizes dense vector weakness on exact codes/SKUs.
commonMistakes: Changing `EMBEDDING_MODEL` in `.env` without re-indexing stored documents!
Expecting semantic embeddings alone to nail exact product IDs, customer IDs, or hex error codes.
Storing vectors with no record of which model generated them.

quizQuestions.prompt: You upgrade your query code from `embed-model-v1` to `embed-model-v2` while leaving existing help-center vectors untouched in your vector DB. What happens to search quality?

options.text: Search relevance collapses into near-random matches because two different embedding models occupy incompatible vector spaces—you must re-embed the index.
options.explanation: Correct! Index and query MUST share the exact same embedding model.

options.text: Accuracy doubles immediately without re-indexing.
options.explanation: Different models produce incompatible vector geometry.

options.text: Vector dimensions auto-translate in Postgres.
options.explanation: Even equal-dimension vectors from distinct models aren't aligned.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Track embedding model versions explicitly and rebuild indexes on upgrades.

quizQuestions.prompt: For which customer query are pure dense semantic embeddings LEAST reliable on their own?

options.text: Exact opaque error code `ERR_WEBHOOK_0x4F2` or part SKU `XJ-904-REV2`.
options.explanation: Correct! Exact string tokens shine with keyword/BM25 search paired alongside vector search (hybrid retrieval).

options.text: Broad semantic paraphrase `'How do I stop future recurring charges?'` matching `'Subscription Cancellation'`.
options.explanation: Paraphrased meaning is precisely where dense embeddings excel.

options.text: Asking `'Can I get my money back?'` matching `'Refund policy'`.
options.explanation: Semantic synonym matching is vector search's forte.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Combine dense semantic vectors with exact keyword search for production robustness.

checkpoints.title: Vector Search
checkpoints.summary: Understand similarity scoring (cosine/dot-product), `top_k`, similarity thresholds, and why 'nearest chunk' doesn't mean 'correct answer'.
learningObjectives: Explain `top_k` similarity retrieval and ANN (Approximate Nearest Neighbor) trade-offs.
Recognize the critical bug: vector DBs ALWAYS return `top_k` neighbors even when zero relevant docs exist!
Separate vector similarity score from factual relevance.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Ask a vector store for `top_k=5` matches for `'What is the capital of Mars?'` against your software Help Center, and it won't say `'Nothing found'` by default—it will faithfully hand back the 5 *least unrelated* paragraphs in your database! If you pass those unrelated chunks into an LLM, you invite weird confabulations. Vector search ranks candidates fast; good systems check thresholds/rerankers AND still allow the LLM to say `'Not covered in docs'`.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Production vector search uses ANN indexes (HNSW, IVF) over cosine similarity or L2/dot-product distance—returning top-`k` candidates in milliseconds (sub-linear scaling with minor recall trade-off configurable via search `ef`/probe params). Crucially: apply metadata ACL filters BEFORE or integrally during ANN search (pre-filtering / single-stage filtered HNSW), NEVER post-filter a tiny `top_k=5` after search (or an entire `top_k` list gets dropped when the user lacks permission on those top hits!).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Post-filtering a tiny `top_k` list leaks fewer docs than zero filtering, yet silently returns 0 results even when authorized docs exist at rank #6!
checkpoints.whenToUse: Use filtered vector similarity (`top_k` calibrated via Recall@K evals) paired with explicit `'no answer in docs'` prompting.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never assume high rank #1 from a vector search means the retrieved chunk actually answers the user's question.

examples.title: Pitfall: Post-Filter Top-K vs Pre-Filtered Search
examples.description: Always pass tenant/audience predicates INTO the index query—never slice afterwards.
examples.code:
BUG (Post-filtering small top_k):
  1. Vector DB returns global top_3 (all belong to Tenant A!)
  2. Python filters `chunk.tenant == 'Tenant B'` -> returns 0 chunks!
  (Even though Tenant B had a perfect matching doc sitting at rank #4!)

FIX (Pre/Integrated Filtered Query):
  Vector DB applies WHERE tenant_id = 'Tenant B' DURING similarity search -> returns Tenant B's top_3!

checkpoints.practiceTask: Explain the bug with post-filtering `top_k=3` in Python after running an unfiltered vector search, and trace how integrated metadata filtering fixes it.
acceptanceCriteria: Knows ANN vector search always returns neighbors unless filtered/thresholded.
Applies ACL filters inside the index query rather than tiny post-filter slices.
Accounts for low-relevance misses with abstention paths.
commonMistakes: Running global `similarity_search(q, k=4)` then filtering `[d for d in docs if d.tenant == tenant]` in Python.
Passing `k=25` unreranked chunks blindly into prompts hoping the LLM sorts it out.
Hardcoding magic cosine thresholds like `score > 0.8` ported blindly from someone else's different embedding model.

quizQuestions.prompt: A customer on Tenant B asks a policy question. Your backend queries global vector search with `k=3`, gets 3 hits belonging to Tenant A, then filters out Tenant A in Python leaving 0 results—even though Tenant B HAS that policy doc! What went wrong?

options.text: Post-filtering a small `top_k` list discards Tenant B hits ranked slightly lower; enforce metadata filters inside the database query itself.
options.explanation: Correct! Pre-filtering / native filtered ANN search inspects only Tenant B's authorized documents.

options.text: Embeddings cannot store Tenant B strings.
options.explanation: Metadata belongs in indexed attributes filtered during retrieval.

options.text: Cosine similarity requires alphabetical tenant names.
options.explanation: Filter placement caused the empty result.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Filter tenant/audience scope inside the retrieval query, not on a tiny post-search slice.

quizQuestions.prompt: Suppose a user asks an out-of-scope question completely absent from your Help Center. What does an unfiltered `top_k=4` vector search return?

options.text: It still returns 4 unrelated 'closest' chunks—so your pipeline must judge relevance or instruct the LLM to abstain clearly.
options.explanation: Correct! Vector stores return nearest neighbors relative to the collection, even when nothing actually answers the question.

options.text: It returns HTTP 404 automatically.
options.explanation: Vector queries return `[]` only if empty index or filters exclude everything.

options.text: It edits the prompt automatically.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

checkpoints.title: Metadata Filtering
checkpoints.summary: Use structured attributes (`tenant_id`, `product`, `audience`, `status`, `updated_at`) to narrow search BEFORE ranking.
learningObjectives: Design crisp indexed metadata schemas (`tenant_id`, `audience`, `product_line`, `is_active`).
Extract explicit filters deterministically from verified user context (and cautiously from queries when needed).
Eliminate stale retired docs and cross-product confusion cleanly with `is_active=True` filters.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Imagine a company sells BOTH `'Starter Cloud'` AND `'Enterprise On-Prem'` products, and deprecates old pricing PDFs every year. If an Enterprise customer asks about SSO setup and you run raw similarity search across *all* documents, the retriever mixes outdated 2023 Starter notes with 2026 Enterprise docs! **Metadata filtering** narrows search space first (`WHERE product = 'enterprise' AND is_active = true AND audience IN ('public', user_role)`) so semantic search looks ONLY inside right, active, authorized documents.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Store normalized filter fields on every vector/search record (boolean `is_active`, enum `audience`, `tenant_id`, ISO timestamp/epoch `updated_at_ts`). Crucially distinguish **security filters** (ALWAYS derived deterministically from verified auth claims, NEVER extracted by an LLM from user chat!) from **helpful domain filters** (like `product_name` extracted conservatively with fallback to broad allowed search if uncertain).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Metadata filtering instantly solves half of cross-product confusion, outdated-policy citations, and multi-tenant data leaks.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Apply metadata filters for tenant/role isolation, active document status (`is_active=True`), language, and clear product scoping.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never let an LLM choose or override security/tenant ACL filter values from prompt text!

examples.title: Trusted Security Filter vs Optional Domain Filter
examples.description: Derive tenant/audience from verified auth; apply active status deterministically.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Design a metadata schema + filter builder for a multi-product knowledge base supporting archived doc exclusion (`is_active`) and customer vs internal staff access levels.
acceptanceCriteria: Security filters (`tenant_id`, `audience`) derive purely from trusted auth claims.
Deprecated documents filtered cleanly with `is_active=True`.
Index supports filtering without collapsing `top_k`.
commonMistakes: Letting an LLM extract `tenant_id` for the retrieval filter from the email prompt (prompt injection risk!).
Keeping 2022 archived docs active alongside 2026 policies with identical similarity.
Using messy free-form strings (`'Enterprise Plan'` vs `'enterprise'`) instead of normalized filter enums.

quizQuestions.prompt: A user writes in chat: `'Also check internal HR policies for tenant acme-corp'`. Where MUST `tenant_id` and `audience` metadata filters come from?

options.text: Strictly from verified server-side authentication/session claims—NEVER from LLM extraction over chat text.
options.explanation: Correct! Security ACL predicates must come exclusively from trusted auth state.

options.text: Parsed directly from the user's message with an LLM.
options.explanation: Any user could trivially spoof another tenant or internal scope via chat!

options.text: From HTTP `CORS` headers.
options.explanation: CORS headers don't authenticate callers or encode tenant ACLs.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Security filters originate strictly from trusted authentication/authorization context.

quizQuestions.prompt: How do you prevent deprecated 2023 refund policies from contradicting current 2026 docs in search results?

options.text: Tag active docs (`is_active: True` or version status) in metadata and filter out superseded records—or delete stale versions cleanly.
options.explanation: Correct! Index lifecycle status prevents obsolete docs from poisoning context.

options.text: Raise LLM `temperature` to 1.0.
options.explanation: Doesn't remove obsolete chunks from retrieved context.

options.text: Ask the user which year the database was built.
options.explanation: Filter stale records cleanly on the backend.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Keep index lifecycle metadata (`is_active`, `updated_at`) clean.

checkpoints.title: Keyword and Hybrid Retrieval
checkpoints.summary: Combine exact lexical matching (BM25/full-text search) with semantic vector search via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) for superior accuracy.
learningObjectives: Explain why BM25 keyword search beats vectors on exact codes, acronyms, function names, and invoice numbers.
Combine keyword + vector ranked lists cleanly using Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).
Spot queries where hybrid retrieval prevents glaring vector misses.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Customer writes: *'Getting webhook error `E_HMAC_MISMATCH` on v2 endpoint.'* Semantic vectors think `'webhook error'` sounds vaguely like twenty general webhook articles, often ranking the exact `E_HMAC_MISMATCH` troubleshooting section at #11! Classic full-text keyword search (**BM25**) spots exact rare terms immediately, while semantic search nails paraphrased concepts (`'billed twice'` -> `'duplicate charge'`). **Hybrid retrieval** runs BOTH and merges the winners cleanly!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Hybrid search queries both sparse/lexical retrieval (BM25 / Postgres `tsvector` GIN full-text) and dense ANN vectors in parallel, merging distinct scoring scales safely without arbitrary normalization hacks via **Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF)**: `score(doc) = Σ 1 / (k + rank_i)` (with constant `k=60`). Hybrid search consistently raises `Recall@K` across enterprise support corpora containing product codes, API fields, and error IDs.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Pure vector demos fail painfully on error codes, customer product names, and exact API route strings—hybrid search fixes that cleanly.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Default to hybrid (BM25/keyword + dense vector + RRF) whenever your corpus mixes natural prose with exact codes, SKUs, config keys, or technical symbols.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't blindly sum raw Postgres `ts_rank` scores with raw cosine similarities without RRF or calibrated normalization—their scales don't match!

examples.title: Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) in 12 Lines of Python
examples.description: Merge incompatible keyword and vector rank lists cleanly without raw score scaling bugs.

checkpoints.practiceTask: Implement `rrf_fuse` above on two sample ranked doc-ID lists (BM25 ranking vs vector ranking) and verify documents appearing near the top of BOTH rise to #1.
acceptanceCriteria: Explains complementary strengths of BM25 (exact terms) vs dense vectors (paraphrases).
Uses RRF (rank-based) rather than naively adding unscaled scores.
Applies same ACL metadata filters across BOTH keyword and vector paths!
commonMistakes: Applying metadata ACL filter to the vector query while forgetting the exact same filter on the BM25/keyword branch (major security leak!).
Adding `bm25_score + cosine_score` raw numbers directly (e.g., `18.4 + 0.78` lets BM25 dominate blindly).
Skipping keyword search completely for technical documentation or support troubleshooting.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why does Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) combine keyword and vector search lists using rank positions (`1 / (60 + rank)`) instead of adding raw BM25 + cosine scores?

options.text: BM25 scores (unbounded positive floats like `0..30`) and cosine scores (`-1..1`) are on incompatible numerical scales; ranks merge fairly across any search methods.
options.explanation: Correct! Rank-based fusion stays clean and scale-invariant.

options.text: Python cannot add two floats from different databases.
options.explanation: Incompatible numeric meaning, not Python math, is the issue.

options.text: RRF translates languages automatically.
options.explanation: RRF fuses ranked results.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Use RRF (or calibrated fusion) to combine keyword and semantic retrieval.

quizQuestions.prompt: What security oversight happens when adding hybrid search if engineers aren't careful?

options.text: Remembering metadata tenant/ACL filters on the vector search leg while forgetting the identical filter on the BM25 keyword leg!
options.explanation: Correct! BOTH retrieval legs must enforce identical access-control filters.

options.text: BM25 slows down Pydantic validators.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

options.text: RRF deletes headers.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Apply identical ACL metadata filters across every retrieval path.

checkpoints.title: Reranking Concepts
checkpoints.summary: Use two-stage retrieval (fast hybrid candidate recall `k=20–40` -> cross-encoder/reranker top `3–5`) to boost precision while keeping prompts lean.
learningObjectives: Contrast bi-encoder independent embeddings (fast retrieval) vs cross-encoder rerankers (joint query+passage relevance).
Apply a 2-stage funnel: recall `top 25` candidates quickly -> rerank -> pass crisp `top 3–5` to LLM.
Weigh reranker latency/cost against prompt token savings and answer quality.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Standard embeddings encode the query and each chunk *separately*—fast across 100,000 docs, though subtle word relationships get compressed! A **reranker (cross-encoder)** reads the query AND one candidate chunk *side-by-side* carefully to judge exact relevance. It's too slow to scan 100,000 docs directly, yet lightning-fast across the top 20–30 hybrid matches—letting you pass just the sharp top 4 chunks into your LLM prompt instead of stuffing 20 noisy chunks!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Two-stage retrieval splits work cleanly: Stage 1 (Candidate Generation via hybrid BM25+ANN, `k=20..40`, maximizing Recall); Stage 2 (Cross-encoder reranker scoring `(query, chunk_text)` jointly, trimming down to `top_n=3..5` high-precision passages). This shrinks LLM prompt size, improves context signal-to-noise ratio, and supplies explicit relevance scores useful for low-confidence abstention thresholds—at modest ~50–150ms Stage 2 overhead.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Precision at the top 3–5 chunks directly controls whether the LLM drafts accurate answers or gets distracted by tangential policy fragments.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Introduce reranking whenever Stage 1 Recall@25 finds the right answer, yet top-4 precision still contains distracting partial matches.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't spend latency adding a heavy remote reranker if Stage 1 Recall@25 misses the right doc completely—fix ingestion/chunking/hybrid search first!

examples.title: Two-Stage Retrieval Pipeline Shape
examples.description: High recall in Stage 1; crisp precision + smaller LLM context in Stage 2.
examples.code:
Query ("double charge refund timeline")
  |-- Stage 1: Hybrid BM25 + Vector (ACL filtered) --> Top 25 candidate chunks (~20ms)
  |-- Stage 2: Cross-Encoder Reranker              --> Re-scores all 25 pairs (~90ms)
  '-- Keep Top 4 high-scoring chunks               --> Assemble grounded prompt (~1,600 tokens vs 10,000!)

options.explanation: Correct! Reranking improves Precision@3 only if Recall@25 already captures the right chunk.

options.text: Yes, rerankers scan deleted files magically.

options.text: Yes, by increasing `temperature`.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

options.text: By safely trimming 20 raw Stage 1 candidates down to the sharpest 3–4 chunks before LLM prefill.
options.explanation: Correct! Fewer, cleaner prompt tokens speed up LLM inference and reduce distraction.

options.text: Because rerankers convert text into PNGs.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

options.text: Rerankers remove HTTPS overhead.
options.explanation: Unrelated.

checkpoints.title: Context Assembly
checkpoints.summary: Order, deduplicate, budget-cap, and delimit retrieved passages cleanly before sending them to the LLM—guarding against prompt bloat and indirect injection.
learningObjectives: Deduplicate overlapping chunks and enforce hard total character/token budgets.
Format each retrieved passage with clear `doc_id`, `section`, and untrusted-data boundaries.
Keep highest-relevance passages prominently positioned rather than buried mid-context.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Retrieving chunks is only half the bridge—next comes **context assembly**: gluing the selected snippets neatly into your prompt without duplicating near-identical overlapping chunks, exceeding context limits, or letting hostile text inside a scraped KB article hijack your instructions. Labeling each block clearly (`[Source: policy_refund_v3 | Section: Annual Plans] ...`) inside `<retrieved_context>` tags gives the LLM clean citation anchors AND respects prompt trust boundaries!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Deterministic context assembly pipeline: (1) deduplicate identical/adjacent overlapping `chunk_id`s; (2) order chunks deliberately (best first or logical document order); (3) enforce strict `max_context_tokens` budget truncation so oversized docs never overflow context; (4) format XML/JSON source wrappers exposing exact citable `doc_id`s alongside explicit system instructions that retrieved passages provide reference facts ONLY (never executable instructions—mitigating indirect prompt injection).
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Clean context wrappers unlock verifiable citations and predictable token spend; messy raw joins create bloated ambiguous prompts.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Route all retrieved chunks through one shared `assemble_context(...)` helper enforcing deduplication, token budget, and clear `[doc_id]` citation labels.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never concatenate 15 unformatted raw chunk strings (`'\n'.join(texts)`) with no source IDs or total length ceiling.

examples.title: Budgeted Context Assembly with Citation Tags
examples.description: Deduplicate chunks, attach verifiable source tags, and respect token/char cap.

acceptanceCriteria: Deduplicates repeated chunks.
Enforces deterministic size/token ceiling.
Attaches verifiable `doc_id` + `section` tags inside delimited retrieved-context block.
commonMistakes: Forgetting `max_chars`/`max_tokens` caps and blowing past model limits when unusually large chunks match.
Joining raw chunks without `doc_id` headers so the LLM literally cannot cite where facts came from.
Placing retrieved external user tickets/wiki pages inside the trusted `system` prompt without delimiters.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why tag every block inside `assemble_context` with `[doc_id=...] [section=...]`?

options.text: So the LLM can reference exact `doc_id` identifiers in structured `citations`, which Python can verify deterministically afterward!
options.explanation: Correct! Explicit ID tags connect retrieved inputs directly to verifiable citations.

options.text: Because embeddings only work with square brackets.
options.explanation: Brackets aid structured grounding and verification.

options.text: To compress tokens via gzip.
options.explanation: Plaintext tags aid attribution, not compression.

quizQuestions.takeaway: Label every retrieved chunk with stable source IDs for downstream citation checks.

quizQuestions.prompt: Why enforce a deterministic character/token ceiling during context assembly even when `top_k=4`?

options.text: If a chunk parser emits unusually long sections or oversized tables, an explicit ceiling guards context windows, latency, and cost predictably.
options.explanation: Correct! Defensive budgeting stops unexpected chunk spikes from overflowing prompts.

options.text: Because Pydantic strings cap at 100 bytes.
options.explanation: Defensive LLM context budgeting prevents unexpected overflow.

options.text: To hide missing data.
options.explanation: Truncation happens safely at chunk boundaries once budget fills.

checkpoints.title: Source Attribution
checkpoints.summary: Require structured citations tied to real retrieved `doc_id`s—and verify in Python that the LLM didn't fabricate fake citation IDs!
learningObjectives: Collect structured `Citation(doc_id, section, quote)` fields alongside answers.
Verify deterministically in Python that EVERY cited `doc_id` was actually present in the retrieved set!
Enable fast human verification during approval workflows.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: When a human support rep reviews an AI-drafted customer reply saying *'Yes, Enterprise customers get a full refund within 45 days'*, they immediately ask: **'Where did you get 45 days?!'** Adding structured **source attribution** lets the UI display exact clickable doc links beside the draft (`policy_enterprise_v2 — Refund Window`)—making human review take 5 seconds instead of 5 minutes. Even better: check in Python that every `doc_id` the LLM cited actually appeared in Stage 1/2 retrieval!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Ask structured outputs for `citations: list[Citation]` containing `doc_id` + brief verbatim `supporting_quote`, then run deterministic Python verification: `[c for c in decision.citations if c.doc_id in retrieved_doc_ids]`. If the LLM fabricates an invalid citation ID (or returns zero citations despite claiming policy specifics), flag for mandatory human inspection rather than displaying unverified citations.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Verifiable citations turn human-in-the-loop review from slow re-research into fast side-by-side verification—and catch hallucinated policy references automatically.

checkpoints.title: Retrieval Evaluation
checkpoints.summary: Measure retrieval independently (`Recall@K`, `MRR`, negative tests) BEFORE tweaking answer prompts—so you fix search bugs at the root.
learningObjectives: Compute `Recall@K` and Mean Reciprocal Rank (`MRR`) on a labeled `(query -> expected_doc_ids)` eval set.
Include unanswerable / negative queries testing whether abstention triggers cleanly.
Separate retriever failure debugging from LLM prompt debugging.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose your RAG support assistant gives 30% bad answers. Should you rewrite the LLM system prompt—or did the vector search simply fail to find the right help doc?! Beginners blindly tweak wording in the prompt for days when the retriever never even pulled the right chunk! Evaluating **retrieval separately** (`Recall@K`: on 40 test questions, how often did the expected doc ID land inside the top `K` chunks?) catches search/chunking bugs deterministically with ZERO LLM generation cost!
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Evaluate retrieval deterministically offline in milliseconds/seconds against labeled pairs `(query, relevant_doc_ids)`: `Recall@K` checks whether at least one ground-truth `doc_id` appears in top `K` (`hits / N`); `MRR` rewards ranking the right doc at #1 over #5. Also evaluate `Faithfulness` and `Answer Relevance` separately during end-to-end generation testing once retrieval Recall@K exceeds target baseline.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Separating retrieval evals from generation evals cuts debugging guesswork in half and gives an instant automated regression gate whenever chunking or embeddings change.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Build a 20–50 query `(question, expected_doc_id)` JSON eval file right alongside your RAG retriever from week one.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Don't test RAG purely by eyeballing 3 answers manually and guessing whether chunking changes helped.

checkpoints.title: Access Control
checkpoints.summary: Prevent confidential cross-tenant or internal-staff document leaks in RAG using strict query-time ACL enforcement.
learningObjectives: Recognize OWASP sensitive-disclosure threats unique to shared RAG indexes.
Enforce verified tenant/role ACL predicates on EVERY retrieval store call.
Write automated negative authorization tests proving Tenant A can NEVER retrieve Tenant B chunks.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Suppose Acme Corp and Beta Inc are both customers on your SaaS platform, OR your knowledge base holds both public Help articles AND private `'Internal Escalation Slack Runbooks (Do Not Share Externally)'`. If a naive RAG index mixes everything together without verified tenant/role access filters, Customer A can ask *'What did Beta Inc complain about?'* or trick the bot into quoting private internal runbooks straight into a public reply! **Every retrieval query must enforce access control at the database layer.**
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Implement document-level / tenant-level ACL enforcement across the entire ingestion and query lifecycle: (1) Embed immutable `tenant_id` and `allowed_roles`/`visibility` fields into vector AND keyword records; (2) Require non-optional `auth_context` on every `retrieve(...)` service method so unauthenticated unfiltered calls cannot even compile/pass type checks; (3) Filter INSIDE the database query (`WHERE tenant_id = :auth_tenant`), never after a tiny `top_k` slice; (4) Add automated cross-tenant access negative unit/integration tests in CI.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: One cross-tenant leak in a RAG chatbot destroys customer trust and violates enterprise compliance contracts instantly.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Mandate explicit verified ACL filtering on every multi-tenant or mixed internal/external RAG system from commit #1.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never expose a single shared unfiltered collection to both internal staff runbooks and customer-facing endpoints, and never derive ACL filters from LLM text.

checkpoints.title: Why RAG Does Not Eliminate Hallucinations
checkpoints.summary: Understand the 5 specific ways RAG systems STILL hallucinate or mislead—and layer verification and abstention to catch them.
learningObjectives: List failure points where RAG still fabricates: missing chunks, conflicting chunks, unfaithful synthesis, chunk truncation, and injected docs.
Contrast 'retrieval grounded' vs 'faithful generation' (did the draft twist what the retrieved chunk actually said?).
Enforce abstention when evidence is missing or conflicting.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Marketing slogans love saying 'Add RAG and hallucinations drop to zero!' Reality check: **RAG lowers blind guessing yet introduces new subtler failures.** If Chunk A says `'2024 price $19'` and Chunk B says `'2026 price $29'`, the LLM may blend or guess the wrong one. Or the retriever misses the exception paragraph, and the model confidently extrapolates `'Yes, eligible'` when the hidden exception excluded annual trials! Good engineers build faithfulness checks and safe `'I could not confirm this policy'` human escalation paths.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Categorize RAG hallucinations rigorously: (1) Retrieval gap -> relevant chunk missed (`Recall@K < 1`), model falls back on pretraining memory; (2) Partial chunk truncation -> exception clause landed in adjacent chunk; (3) Stale index conflict -> contradictory old/new versions retrieved together; (4) Unfaithful synthesis -> retrieved chunk says X, model extrapolates Y beyond text; (5) Indirect prompt injection hidden inside indexed documents. Mitigate via explicit system abstention instructions, version filtering (`is_active`), full-section chunks, faithfulness eval checks, and human review on high-stakes outputs.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Overconfidence that 'RAG = solved truth' causes teams to auto-send risky policy or legal advice without oversight.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Always prompt explicitly for grounded abstention, check retrieval + faithfulness separately in evals, and gate external customer policy answers with review.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never market or deploy a RAG pipeline as 'zero hallucination' without human safeguards.

checkpoints.title: Document Updates and Deletion
checkpoints.summary: Keep RAG indexes synchronized cleanly when source documents are edited, archived, or deleted—never leave ghost deleted chunks behind!
learningObjectives: Implement atomic/idempotent document sync: track `doc_id` -> old `chunk_id`s, upsert new hash versions, and delete obsolete chunks cleanly.
Support 'Right to be Forgotten' / compliance deletion immediately across indexes.
Prevent duplicate stale + fresh chunks coexisting for the same edited article.
checkpoints.plainEnglishExplanation: Tutorials show how to `insert()` PDF chunks into a vector store on Day 1—and stop there! On Day 14, Finance updates the refund window from 30 days to 14 days, or Legal deletes a discontinued partner document. If your sync script simply re-embeds and inserts the updated PDF *without deleting that document's old chunks*, your RAG bot now contains BOTH `30 days` AND `14 days` simultaneously! Clean indexing tracks `doc_id` ownership so edits replace old chunks atomically and deletions purge all chunks completely.
checkpoints.technicalExplanation: Implement deterministic chunk IDs or `source_doc_id` foreign indexing in your vector/search store. On sync event (`doc_id`, `new_hash`): (1) skip if `new_hash == stored_hash`; (2) otherwise insert/upsert new chunks (optionally under new `version` then flip/delete old version for zero-downtime consistency); (3) delete all chunks matching `doc_id` where `version != current_version`; (4) expose explicit `delete_document(doc_id)` / `delete_tenant(tenant_id)` endpoints hooked to CMS webhooks or scheduled reconciliation sweeps.
checkpoints.whyItMatters: Stale zombie chunks are one of the sneakiest bugs in production RAG—silent contradictions appear weeks after content edits.
checkpoints.whenToUse: Design `doc_id`-keyed replacement, deletion, and content-hash skipping from the very first indexing script.
checkpoints.whenNotToUse: Never run blind `add_documents()` cron jobs that append duplicates of unchanged/edited docs every night!

examples.title: Idempotent Replace & Delete Sync Flow
examples.description: Prevent duplicate chunks and ghost policies across updates.
examples.code:
def sync_document(doc: CleanSourceDoc, store) -> str:
    existing_hash = store.get_doc_hash(doc.doc_id)
    if existing_hash == doc.content_hash:
        return "unchanged_skipped"

    new_chunks = build_chunks_for_doc(doc)  # Tagged with doc.doc_id & doc.content_hash
    store.upsert_chunks(new_chunks)
    # Delete all chunks belonging to this doc_id from older hashes!
    store.delete_stale_chunks(doc_id=doc.doc_id, keep_hash=doc.content_hash)
    return "updated"

def hard_delete_document(doc_id: str, store) -> None:
    store.delete_all_by_doc_id(doc_id)
